title: Sen. Rand Paul opposes Trump's Syria airstrikes: ‘The United States was not attacked’
text: Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul warned President Donald Trump against making war in Syria on Thursday evening, shortly after it was announced that the Pentagon had fired more than 50 Tomahawk cruise missiles at a Syrian air base. “While we all condemn the atrocities in Syria, the United States was not attacked. The President needs congressional authorization for military action as required by the Constitution, and I call on him to come to Congress for a proper debate,” said Paul, who competed against Trump for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination. “Our prior interventions in this region have done nothing to make us safer and Syria will be no different,” he said. Earlier on Thursday, the senator told Brian Kilmeade on Fox News Radio that he doubted the President's ability to change Syria through new attacks. “If he decides to do something in Syria, he would come to Congress and ask for a declaration of war. Short of congress voting on it, I’m opposed to illegal and unconstitutional wars,” he said. “I have the greatest amount of sympathy, I can’t see those pictures, it’s heartrending to see those pictures,” he said. “But going to war we have to decide will it be better or worse? Will we improve our national security? Are we threatened currently by Syria, and if we go to war is Assad likely to use less chemical weapons or more?” Paul argued that American attacks could worsen the situation in Syria. “There’s some argument for the more cornered and the more defeated in some ways more likely they are to use chemical weapons and actually for the less defeated they are that they’re less likely to use them,” he said. “The bottom line is it’s horrific.”

title: U.S. senators press Mylan over EpiPen price hikes
text: Two senior members of the U.S. Senate's Judiciary Committee on Monday sought information about steep price increases for EpiPens, drug-filled injectable devices that people use to counter potentially deadly allergic reactions. Senator Chuck Grassley, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, wrote on Monday to Mylan Chief Executive Heather Bresch asking how Mylan set the price of EpiPens and what changes had been made to the product to justify the higher price. Senator Amy Klobuchar, the top Democrat on the committee's antitrust subcommittee, on Monday urged the Federal Trade Commission to investigate the prices, citing news reports that the price of a two-pack of EpiPens had risen from $100 in 2008 to $500 this year. Mylan acquired the product in 2007. “Although the antitrust laws do not prohibit price gouging, regardless of how unseemly it may be, they do prohibit the use of unreasonable restraints of trade to facilitate or protect a price increase,” wrote Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat who said her daughter relies on an EpiPen. “The FTC should investigate whether Mylan Pharmaceuticals engaged in activity, such as using incentives or exclusionary contracts with insurers, distributors, or pharmacies, to deny an alternative product access to the market.” An EpiPen injects a pre-measured dose of epinephrine (adrenaline), which people use when they are having a dangerous allergic reaction. The FTC did not say whether an investigation was under way. “The commission takes seriously its obligation to take action where pharmaceutical companies have violated the antitrust laws,” a spokesman said. Mylan did not immediately comment on the letters but said in an email that nearly 80 percent of people with commercial insurance who use a savings card can get the medicine for free.

title: Thousands in Romania protest against judicial overhaul
text: Thousands of Romanians braved freezing weather across the country on Sunday to protest against attempts by the ruling Social Democrats to overhaul the judiciary, changes that critics said would threaten the rule of law. In Bucharest, an estimated 4,000 protesters marched from government headquarters to parliament, where lawmakers will start debating changes to the criminal code on Monday. Earlier this month the Social Democrats used their solid majority to push a judicial overhaul through the lower house that threatens to put the justice system under political control. The senate is expected to approve the bills next week. The European Commission, the U.S. State Department, the country's centrist president and thousands of magistrates have criticized the changes to judicial legislation, saying they could derail the rule of law. The government denies this. Outside parliament, marchers chanted “Thieves' nest” and “We want justice, not corruption” in sleet and rain. Thousands more protested in Iasi, Cluj, Timisoara and other cities. The ruling Social Democrats have tried on and off throughout 2017 to change anti-corruption legislation in one of the European Union's most corrupt states. Since 2006, Romania's anti-corruption prosecution unit has sent 72 deputies and senators to trial, along with cabinet ministers, a sitting Prime Minister and hundreds of mayors and other public officials. The speakers of parliament's lower house and senate are both currently on trial in separate cases.

title: Ginsburg hopes 'cooler heads' will prevail over Supreme Court vacancy
text: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said on Wednesday that she hoped “cooler heads will prevail” over the Supreme Court vacancy, suggesting that Republicans should act on President Barack Obama's nominee. Ginsburg spoke at Georgetown Law Center a day after Democrats in the Republican-controlled Senate renewed their push for a confirmation hearing for Obama's choice, appeals court judge Merrick Garland. The nomination has been pending for 175 days without Senate action, the longest ever for the high court. Republicans have said the next president should make the appointment because the vacancy, created when conservative Justice Antonin Scalia died in February, arose in the final year of Obama's presidency. “I do think that cooler heads will prevail, I hope sooner rather than later,” Ginsburg said. Ginsburg, 83, a liberal appointed by Democratic President Bill Clinton in 1993, acknowledged that the Senate, which is responsible for confirming or rejecting judicial nominations, was not required to confirm the nominee. But she said it did have an obligation at least to consider Garland rather than do nothing at all. “The president is elected for four years, not three years,” she said, referring to the president's authority to make appointments in the last year of a term. “Maybe some members of the Senate will wake up and appreciate that that’s how it should be.” Earlier on Wednesday, Democratic senators held a press conference outside the Supreme Court demanding action on the nomination. But Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has so far stuck to his pledge to take no action. The nine-seat court has been one justice short since Scalia died.

title: Kansas City man freed after 17 years in prison when his lookalike is found
text: A Kansas City man has been released after serving 17 years behind bars for a robbery he did not commit, after a man who looked so much like him that they could be twins was finally found and brought to the court's attention. Richard Anthony Jones was convicted of a Roeland Park robbery committed in 1999, but from the first day of his arrest Jones maintained that he was innocent. While in prison, he began hearing from other inmates that he bore a striking resemblance to another known criminal. After years of pleading his case, Jones, who had been convicted solely on eyewitness testimony, finally got help from the Innocence Project, which believed him enough to start looking into the claim that a doppelganger may have been the real culprit, the Kansas City Star reported. Jones's lawyers looked into the inmates' story and believed they had found the man everyone said looked so much like their client that the two could pass as the same person. “We were floored by how much they looked alike,” Jones's attorney Alice Craig said of seeing the other man, who some believe committed the crime instead of Jones. The legal team then asked the robbery victim to look at photos of the two men. The photos show each of them with braided hair and a goatee, and the two look so alike that they could easily be mistaken for two photos of the same man. The victim agreed that she could not tell the men apart and could no longer be sure of her testimony. Jones was arrested in 1999 after the victim picked him out of a police photo database.

title: Gorsuch seeks to place himself above politics at confirmation hearing
text: Judge Neil M. Gorsuch on Monday presented himself as a creature of consensus at a sharply partisan Supreme Court confirmation hearing, which was overshadowed throughout by the bitter nomination battle that preceded it over the past year. Democrats, fuming from the hearing's opening moments, made it clear that they would not let the public forget Judge Merrick B. Garland, President Barack Obama's nominee last year, whom Republicans refused even to consider at a hearing, arguing that the seat should be filled by the winner of the presidential election. But when his turn came, Judge Gorsuch repeatedly reached for comity in a speech, insisting that he placed no party above the law and appearing to brace for attacks from critics who say his rulings lean toward corporate interests. “I’ve ruled for disabled students, for prisoners, for the accused, for workers alleging civil rights violations and for undocumented immigrants,” he told the Senate Judiciary Committee. “Sometimes, too, I’ve ruled against such persons.” Opening four days of planned hearings on Judge Gorsuch's nomination, Monday's proceedings — light on direct confrontation, heavy on senatorial windiness — outlined the debates to come: Democrats raised questions about Judge Gorsuch's record on issues such as workers' rights and voiced concerns about President Trump's often dim view of the judicial branch. Republicans sought to shield the jurist, whom they hope to install as the court's next conservative stalwart. And Judge Gorsuch went to great lengths to position himself above politics, on the eve of formal, rigorous questioning from senators on Tuesday. Leaning heavily on biography in his speech, Judge Gorsuch portrayed himself as a humble Westerner who had served with malice toward none during his decade as a federal appellate court judge based in Denver.

title: Kaine's tough-on-crime record may hamper Clinton's outreach to black voters
text: Democrat Hillary Clinton's choice of Tim Kaine as her vice presidential running mate could hinder her efforts to reach African-American voters because of Kaine's past support for crime-fighting strategies that have driven up the U.S. prison population and are unpopular in the black community. The now-defunct Project Exile that Kaine supported was so unusual that it was championed by Republicans and Democrats alike, and by both the top U.S. gun lobby group and gun-control advocates. But the federal program, launched in 1997 in Richmond, Virginia, was also criticized at the time as a racially biased initiative that sentenced young black men to lengthy prison terms. Clinton herself has faced criticism from black activists for her past backing of the tough-on-crime policies of the 1990s, which are now blamed for a surge in the U.S. prison population and heightened tensions between law enforcement and black communities. Earlier this year, one of her fundraisers was disrupted by activists who asked her to “apologize for mass incarceration.” Clinton named Kaine as her running mate late on Friday, in what is regarded as a safe choice for her contest against Republican presidential rival Donald Trump. As Richmond mayor from 1998 to 2001, Kaine, 58, was an outspoken supporter of Project Exile, crediting it with lowering the city's murder rate. Its aim was to live up to its name literally by making illegal gun possession a federal rather than a state crime, which let prosecutors send convicted felons, most of them black, to a distant federal penitentiary for at least five years. Sam Sinyangwe, co-founder of Campaign Zero, a group focused on reducing police violence, said the choice of Kaine could worsen Clinton's difficulties in rallying African-American support, especially among younger people.

title: At the Rio Olympics, does the national anthem sound … sad?
text: When the United States' national anthem plays at Olympic medal ceremonies here, it is bringing American athletes to tears. Elsewhere, the song is producing a very different reaction. “It is driving me crazy,” said Jason DeBord, who lives in Ann Arbor, Mich. “I hit the mute button, or I make dinner, or I just sit there and brace myself.” DeBord has nothing against displays of patriotism, and he is not simply impatient to get back to the action. What bothers him is the version of “The Banner” being used at the Olympics. To put it bluntly, it has been butchered. O.K., that may overstate the problem. It might be more accurate to say that the song has been changed in ways that strip it of its oomph, its power and its optimistic essence. Specifically, DeBord said, this “Banner” shifts several times to minor chords, which in the Western canon are regarded as melancholic, in places where major chords, which are heartier and more upbeat, are normally used. The result, DeBord said, is a rendition of the anthem that is darker and sadder. “It has a totally different emotional feel,” he said. “It is supposed to have an ascending chord structure. Instead, it sort of has a descending chord structure.” In short, this is a defeatist “Banner,” and it is broadcast around the world at a moment of ecstatic international triumph. DeBord, who spent 16 years on Broadway as a conductor and pianist, teaches in the department of musical theater at the University of Michigan. He is the first to admit that few people are likely to notice, let alone be bothered by, the aspects of the song that irritate him.

title: Bahrain introduces entry visas for Qatari nationals and residents
text: Bahrain said on Tuesday that it would require entry visas for Qatari nationals and residents, describing the move as a security measure. In June, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt severed diplomatic, transport and trade ties with Qatar, accusing it of financing terrorism. Doha denies the charge and says the boycott is an attempt to curb its support for reform. “The new measures aim at preventing harming the security and stability of the kingdom of Bahrain particularly in light of the latest repercussions of the crisis with Qatar,” said a statement from the official Bahraini news agency BNA. Citizens of the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council countries are supposed to be able to travel within the GCC with only an identity card. Bahrain's visa requirements will take effect from Nov. 10. title: South Africa's Tutu urges Myanmar's Suu Kyi to help Rohingya
text: Archbishop Desmond Tutu, the retired South African cleric and anti-apartheid campaigner, on Thursday urged Myanmar leader and fellow Nobel Laureate Aung San Suu Kyi to step in to help Rohingya Muslims fleeing her country. Western critics have accused Suu Kyi of failing to speak out for the Rohingya, who have been fleeing to neighboring Bangladesh after an army counter-offensive against militant attacks. In an open letter to Suu Kyi, Tutu said: “I am now elderly, decrepit and formally retired, but breaking my vow to remain silent on public affairs out of profound sadness about the plight of the Muslim minority in your country, the Rohingya. My dear sister: If the political price of your ascension to the highest office in Myanmar is your silence, the price is surely too steep ... We pray for you to speak out for justice, human rights and the unity of your people. We pray for you to intervene,” Tutu wrote. Tutu, 85, has lived with prostate cancer for nearly two decades and has largely withdrawn from public life. The Rohingya number some 1.1 million people who have long complained of persecution and are regarded by many in Buddhist-majority Myanmar as illegal migrants from Bangladesh. “We have to take care of our citizens, we have to take care of everybody who is in our country, whether or not they are our citizens,” Suu Kyi said earlier on Thursday in comments to Asian News International, the Indian partner of Reuters Television. Suu Kyi, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 as a champion of democracy, did not specifically mention the exodus of the minority Rohingya.
